messages.kimi:
feat: Add destroy() method to properly clean up ZeRO-3 hooks and optimizer

Add destroy() method to DeepSpeedEngine and DeepSpeedZeroOptimizer_Stage3 to properly clean up module hooks when reloading saved optimizer. This fixes the error when loading saved optimizer after training with ZeRO-3, where persistent forward/backward hooks from the previous optimizer instance would interfere with the new instance.

The changes:
- Add destroy() method to DeepSpeedEngine that calls optimizer.destroy() if available
- Track forward_hooks and backward_hooks lists in ZeRO-3 optimizer
- Add destroy() method to ZeRO-3 that removes all registered module hooks
- Modify setup_zero_stage3_hooks() to store hook handles for later cleanup

Fixes #1940
messages.claude:
feat: add destroy() to ZeRO-3 for cleaning up module hooks on optimizer reload

What:
- Add `destroy()` to `DeepSpeedEngine` that delegates to the optimizer's
  `destroy()` when present.
- Add `destroy()` to `ZeroStage3` that removes registered forward/backward
  module hooks, and track hook handles in `self.forward_hooks` /
  `self.backward_hooks` during `setup_zero_stage3_hooks()`.
- Log the number of created and deleted hooks via `print_rank_0`.

Why:
Issue #1940 reports errors when reloading a saved optimizer after
training with ZeRO-3. When a new `DeepSpeedEngine` is constructed to
load a checkpoint for evaluation, previously registered forward/backward
hooks from the training-stage optimizer are left attached to the
modules, causing conflicts and failures during the reload path. The
engine had no way to tear down an existing optimizer's state before the
new one is installed. By exposing `destroy()` and removing the ZeRO-3
hooks (and any optimizer-level resources) prior to constructing a new
optimizer/engine, stale hooks are cleaned up deterministically, allowing
the saved optimizer to be loaded cleanly on top of an already-wrapped
ZeRO-3 model.
messages.minimax:
fix: add destroy method to properly cleanup ZeRO-3 hooks and optimizer state

What: Added `destroy()` methods to `DeepSpeedEngine` and `ZeroStage3` classes to properly remove module hooks and cleanup optimizer state. Changed hook registration in `ZeroStage3` to store hook references instead of discarding them.

Why: When reloading a saved optimizer after training with ZeRO-3, existing hooks and optimizer state can cause errors. The `register_forward_pre_hook` and `register_forward_hook` calls returned hook handles that were never stored or removed, leaving dangling references. This fix ensures hooks are properly tracked and removed on destroy, preventing errors when loading checkpoints for evaluation. This addresses issue #1940 where loading a saved optimizer after training failed with ZeRO-3.

messages.kimi:
fix: Fix AttributeError when parameter offloading to NVME is enabled

Fix the 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'reserve_partitioned_swap_space' error that occurs when using parameter offloading to NVME with ZeRO Stage 3. The issue was caused by partitioned parameters not being properly initialized with the DeepSpeed configuration before the swap space reservation.

Changes include:
- Pass ds_config to ZeRO Stage 3 optimizer initialization to ensure proper configuration propagation
- Refactor offloading configuration into a separate _configure_offloading method for better code organization
- Update _convert_to_zero_parameters to accept ds_config and pass it to Init, along with remote_device and pin_memory settings
- Fix parameter status tracking in swap_out_partitioned_params to set status to NOT_AVAILABLE after swap out

This ensures that when params_in_nvme_and_cpu is enabled, the partitioned parameter initialization has access to the full DeepSpeed configuration needed for NVME swap space management.
messages.claude:
feat: enable ZeRO parameter initialization with NVME/CPU offloading configuration

What:
- Pass ds_config into ZeroStage3.__init__ and forward it to Init() along
  with remote_device and pin_memory so non-zero parameters can be
  converted with the correct offload target (NVME, CPU, or none).
- Extract offload optimizer/param setup into _configure_offloading() and
  invoke it before _convert_to_zero_parameters(), so params_in_nvme_and_cpu
  and offload_param are known at parameter-conversion time.
- In partitioned_param_swapper.swap_out_partitioned_params, mark
  dst_fp16_params' ds_tensor.status as NOT_AVAILABLE after swap-out to
  keep partitioned status consistent with the async swap pool.

Why:
Fixes #1543. When params were offloaded to NVME, Init() was called
without a remote_device, so no partitioned swap space was reserved on
the parameter tensors. The subsequent optimizer swap path then called
reserve_partitioned_swap_space on a None swapper/missing tensor,
raising "'NoneType' object has no attribute 'reserve_partitioned_swap_space'".

Configuring offloading before parameter conversion and propagating the
remote device through Init() ensures partitioned swap buffers are
allocated up front, so the optimizer swapper can reserve and use them.
The post-swap-out status fix prevents downstream code from reading
params that are mid-flight in the async swap pool.

Pass ds_config through the initialization chain so that param offloading is correctly configured when enabled. Also fix the partitioned param status not being set to NOT_AVAILABLE after swap-out, which caused a NoneType error when NVME offloading was active.

Issue #7918: Fork safety
It looks like deepspeed is not fork-safe:

- During import it checks `builder.is_compatible()` for all ops
- Some ops use `torch.cuda.get_device_properties`
- This initializes the CUDA context

See https://github.com/deepspeedai/DeepSpeed/blob/38bd11a758875cc48b9def31c74464140658ce43/deepspeed/git_version_info.py#L30

When the process then forks to run in parallel any access to CUDA through PyTorch will fail:
> RuntimeError: Cannot re-initialize CUDA in forked subprocess. To use CUDA with multiprocessing, you must use the 'spawn' start method


I'm not sure why this doesn't seem to be fully consistent but I can reproduce it with:
`pytest --forked tests/unit/ops/deepspeed4science/test_DS4Sci_EvoformerAttention.py -k 'test_DS4Sci_EvoformerAttention[tensor_shape1-dtype1]' -s`

Where it will fail when invoking `skip_on_arch(8 if dtype == torch.bfloat16 else 7)` which calls `torch.cuda.get_device_properties`, now in the forked subprocess.


This is an issue in general: Fork-multiprocessing can not be used after importing deepspeed

But it also contradicts the [documentation](https://github.com/deepspeedai/DeepSpeed/blob/master/docs/contributing.md):
> Note that [pytest-forked](https://github.com/pytest-dev/pytest-forked) and the --forked flag are required to test CUDA functionality in distributed tests.

It seems the opposite is true: The flag must not be used.

Or am I missing anything?

messages.kimi:
fix: Prevent CUDA context initialization during import to enable fork-safe multiprocessing (#7918)

Set PYTORCH_NVML_BASED_CUDA_CHECK=1 in deepspeed/__init__.py before importing torch to avoid creating a CUDA context at import time. Refactor op builders to use a new cuda_capability_major() method that only probes device properties when a CUDA context already exists, preventing fork() poisoning. Update ds_transformer.py to gate Triton imports on HAS_TRITON alone rather than also checking is_triton_supported() at import time. Update documentation in CONTRIBUTING.md and docs/contributing.md to clarify that --forked is now safe to use. Add comprehensive tests to verify fork safety after importing deepspeed.
messages.claude:
fix: make `import deepspeed` fork-safe by deferring CUDA context creation

Issue #7918 reports that importing DeepSpeed is not fork-safe: during
import the builder `is_compatible()` path calls
`torch.cuda.get_device_properties(0)`, which lazily initializes a CUDA
context in the parent process. After `fork()`, the child cannot reuse
that context and fails with
`RuntimeError: Cannot re-initialize CUDA in forked subprocess`, breaking
fork-based multiprocessing (and contradicting the docs, which say
`pytest --forked` is required for CUDA tests).

What:
- Set `PYTORCH_NVML_BASED_CUDA_CHECK=1` (via `setdefault` to preserve an
  explicit user setting) at the top of `deepspeed/__init__.py`, before
  importing torch, so PyTorch's CUDA availability check uses NVML and
  does not create a CUDA context.
- Drop the `get_accelerator().is_triton_supported()` gate from the
  triton kernel import in `ds_transformer.py`; it read GPU compute
  capability at import time and created a context. Triton use is still
  gated at runtime via `self.config.use_triton`.
- Add `CUDAOpBuilder.cuda_capability_major()`, a side-effect-free probe
  that returns `None` unless a CUDA context already exists and we are
  not inside a bad fork. Replace direct
  `torch.cuda.get_device_properties(0).major` calls in
  `evoformer_attn`, `fp_quantizer`, `inference_core_ops`,
  `inference_cutlass_builder`, `ragged_ops`, `ragged_utils`,
  `spatial_inference`, and `transformer_inference` builders with this
  helper, treating `None` as "skip the compute-capability check and defer
  it to build/load time".
- Update `CONTRIBUTING.md` and `docs/contributing.md` to explain why
  `--forked` is safe now that `import deepspeed` no longer initializes a
  CUDA context.
- Add unit tests in `tests/unit/ops/test_op_builder.py` covering the new
  helper's three branches (no context, context already initialized, bad
  fork) and an end-to-end subprocess test asserting a forked child can
  still use CUDA after the parent runs `import deepspeed`.

Why: importing a library should not have the side effect of initializing
CUDA in the parent process, since that poisons `fork()`-based
multiprocessing for any downstream user. Deferring the context creation
until it is actually needed (op build/load, or runtime use) restores
fork safety and makes the documented `pytest --forked` workflow correct.
messages.minimax:
fix: prevent CUDA context creation during `import deepspeed` to preserve fork() safety

Issue #7918: importing DeepSpeed initialized a CUDA context via `torch.cuda.get_device_properties()` calls during op compatibility checks. This poisoned fork()-based multiprocessing because a forked child cannot re-initialize CUDA.

Changes:
- Set `PYTORCH_NVML_BASED_CUDA_CHECK=1` at import time so PyTorch uses NVML-based device queries that never create a CUDA context
- Added `CUDAOpBuilder.cuda_capability_major()` that returns `None` instead of probing when no context exists or when inside a bad fork, deferring the check to build/load time
- Updated all `is_compatible()` implementations to use the new method with `None`-safe guards
- Removed `is_triton_supported()` gate from triton kernel imports (was reading GPU compute capability at import time)
- Updated CONTRIBUTING.md and docs/contributing.md to note `--forked` is now safe

```python
messages.kimi:
fix: Fix dtype mismatch in ZeRO-3 _allgather_params_coalesced for mixed-type parameter lists

Fixes #8072

The _allgather_params_coalesced method incorrectly used param_list[0].ds_tensor.dtype for all tensors in the coalesced all-gather operation. When using ZeRO Stage 3 with PEFT (LoRA), parameters in the list can have different dtypes (e.g., bfloat16 base model weights vs float32 LoRA adapter weights). This caused a "TypeError: output tensor must have the same type as input tensor" error during the optimizer step when all-gathering persistent parameters.

Changed to use enumerate to track the index and correctly reference each parameter's own dtype (param_list[i].ds_tensor.dtype) when creating the flat tensor for all-gather, ensuring dtype consistency for each individual parameter.
messages.claude:
fix: use per-parameter dtype in _allgather_params_coalesced

When collecting flat tensors for the all-gather of partitioned
parameters, the code unconditionally took the dtype from
`param_list[0].ds_tensor.dtype`. With ZeRO Stage 3 + PEFT (LoRA) on a
bfloat16 base model, the adapter parameters created by PEFT default to a
different dtype (e.g. float32) than the base parameters. Because every
flat tensor was allocated with the dtype of the first parameter in the
list, parameters whose dtype did not match `param_list[0]` ended up
being all-gathered into a tensor of the wrong type, raising
`TypeError: output tensor must have the same type as input tensor` in
`_allgather_params_coalesced` during `_post_step`. This regression
appeared in 0.19.2 and breaks training on the first optimizer step.

Track each parameter's own dtype by enumerating `partition_sizes` and
using `param_list[i].ds_tensor.dtype` for the corresponding flat
tensor, so the all-gather output type always matches its input
parameter. This restores compatibility with mixed-dtype parameter
groups such as LoRA adapters on bf16 base models.

Fixes #8072
messages.minimax:
Fix dtype mismatch in _allgather_params_coalesced for ZeRO-3 + PEFT

When using ZeRO Stage 3 with PEFT LoRA adapters on bfloat16 base models (e.g. Qwen2, Llama 3), a TypeError was raised during _post_step. The root cause is that `param_list[0].ds_tensor.dtype` was used unconditionally instead of the dtype corresponding to each parameter at index `i` in the loop. This caused a dtype mismatch when persistent parameters have different dtypes across partitions. Fixes the regression introduced in 0.19.2 (issue #8072).
```

```
Issue #7807: [BUG] Cross-partition parameters incorrectly updated when using ZeRO-1/ZeRO-2 with reduce_scatter=true and Muon optimizer
**Describe the bug**

When using the Muon optimizer with ZeRO-1 or ZeRO-2 and `reduce_scatter=true`, parameters that span partition boundaries receive incorrect gradient updates due to incomplete gradient reduction before orthogonalization. This causes the Newton-Schulz orthogonalization in Muon to operate on partially reduced gradients, leading to incorrect parameter updates for cross-partition parameters.

**To Reproduce**

Steps to reproduce the behavior:

1. Set up a training configuration with:
   - ZeRO stage 1 or 2 with `reduce_scatter: true` in the DeepSpeed config
   - Muon optimizer (or MuonWithAuxAdam) for 2D weight matrices
   - Multi-GPU training (e.g., 4 GPUs)

2. Run training and observe that some parameters (those crossing partition boundaries) receive inconsistent gradient updates across ranks


**Expected behavior**

All ranks should receive fully reduced gradients before Muon's orthogonalization step, ensuring that:
- The Newton-Schulz iteration operates on complete, correctly reduced gradients
- All ranks compute identical orthogonalized updates for the same parameter
- Cross-partition parameters are updated consistently
```

Looking at the code changes, I can see this is adding a new test class `TestMuonZero12NumericalCorrectness` that validates Muon optimizer's Newton-Schulz orthogonalization runs on the full DP-averaged gradient under ZeRO-1/2. This is a test addition to catch a specific bug (#7807) where cross-partition parameters were incorrectly updated.

Based on the type definitions and reference examples, this falls under test category since it's adding new test code to verify/fix a regression.

test: Add numerical correctness test for Muon optimizer with ZeRO-1/2

Add TestMuonZero12NumericalCorrectness regression test for issue #7807 where cross-partition parameters received incorrect gradient updates when using ZeRO-1/ZeRO-2 with reduce_scatter=true. The test validates that Muon's Newton-Schulz orthogonalization runs on the full DP-averaged gradient by comparing the applied update against an independent reference that applies muon_update to the full averaged gradient. This catches the partition-then-orthogonalize bug which diverges by O(1) versus the expected small rounding error from fp16/bf16 precision.
messages.minimax:
test: add numerical-correctness regression test for #7807 Muon ZeRO-1/2 bug

Add TestMuonZero12NumericalCorrectness to catch the partition-then-orthogonalize
bug in Muon under ZeRO-1/2. The existing Muon tests only assert that parameters
changed, which cannot detect a wrong-but-nonzero update. The new test runs on >=2
ranks with a 2D weight that straddles the gradient-partition boundary (the exact
case #7807 corrupts), and compares the applied Muon update against an independent
reference that applies the real muon_update to the full averaged gradient. A
partition-then-orthogonalize bug diverges by O(1), far above fp16/bf16 numerical
rounding, so a threshold of 0.40 robustly separates the buggy from correct behavior
for both gram and standard ns_method variants.
messages.claude:
test: add Muon ZeRO-1/2 numerical-correctness regression for #7807

Add TestMuonZero12NumericalCorrectness, a distributed (world_size=2)
regression test that verifies Muon's Newton-Schulz orthogonalization
runs on the FULL DP-averaged gradient under ZeRO-1/2 with
reduce_scatter=False.

Why:
Issue #7807 reported that cross-partition 2D weights receive corrupted
updates when Muon orthogonalizes a partition slice instead of the full
averaged gradient. The existing Muon tests only assert that parameters
changed, which cannot distinguish a wrong-but-nonzero update from a
correct one, so the regression went undetected.

How:
- Size the model so a 2D Muon weight straddles the rank-0/rank-1
  partition boundary (exactly the case #7807 corrupts); assert that
  precondition so the test fails fast rather than silently passing.
- Run a deterministic global batch where each rank's slice averages to
  the full-batch gradient, then compare the engine's applied update
  against an independent reference computed via muon_update on the full
  gradient.
- Disable gradient clipping and use a static loss scale so the applied
  update equals -lr*muon_update(grad) for an exact comparison.
- Parametrize over ns_method ('gram','standard') and zero_stage (1,2).
  A partition-then-orthogonalize bug diverges by O(1) (measured
  ~0.6-0.67), while legitimate fp16 NS rounding stays at ~0.07 (gram)
  / ~0.22 (standard); the 0.40 threshold separates both robustly.

```
messages.kimi:
fix: Prevent Muon optimizer from being used with reduce_scatter in ZeRO-1/2 (#7807)

Muon's Newton-Schulz orthogonalization requires the full all-reduced gradient matrix on each rank to compute correct updates. When reduce_scatter is enabled in ZeRO-1/2, each rank only receives its own partition slice of the gradient, causing the orthogonalization to silently corrupt parameters that span partition boundaries. This change adds an explicit guard in stage_1_and_2.py that raises ValueError during initialization when MuonWithAuxAdam is used with reduce_scatter, matching the existing protection in ZeRO-3 (stage3.py). A test is added to verify the error is properly raised for both ZeRO-1 and ZeRO-2 configurations.
messages.claude:
fix: reject Muon optimizer when reduce_scatter is enabled in ZeRO-1/2

Muon's Newton-Schulz orthogonalization requires the full all-reduced
gradient matrix on each rank. With reduce_scatter enabled, ZeRO-1/2
only delivers each rank its own partition slice, so the orthogonalization
silently operates on partially reduced gradients and corrupts cross-partition
parameter updates (#7807). ZeRO-3 already guards against this in stage3.py
(see #7919), but the same misconfiguration was still accepted at ZeRO-1/2
initialization.

Add an explicit ValueError in stage_1_and_2.py when MuonWithAuxAdam is
combined with reduce_scatter, so users fail loudly instead of silently
producing divergent updates across ranks. Cover the guard with a new
test_muon_reduce_scatter_raises test for both stage 1 and stage 2.
messages.minimax:
fix: reject reduce_scatter with Muon optimizer in ZeRO-1/2

Muon's Newton-Schulz orthogonalization requires the full all-reduced gradient
on each rank, but reduce_scatter delivers only the partition slice. This
silently corrupts cross-partition parameters in ZeRO-1/2 (issue #7807).

Add a guard at initialization that raises ValueError when MuonWithAuxAdam
is used with reduce_scatter=true, consistent with the ZeRO-3 guard in
stage3.py (added in #7919).
```

```

**To Reproduce**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. Use large model to run, or set sub_group_size to a lower value. Then train and save model
2. Run ds_to_universal.py

**The reason**

I found that the previous stage3 universal checkpoint implementation did not take subgroups into account. I also found the following problems during debugging.

* Unable to handle multiple sub-groups, which will result in data loss
* When load_checkpoint is True, then all process will save to same zero model checkpoint file. If multiple processes write at the same time, the file will be corrupted. Occasionally, file corruption was discovered during testing.

messages.kimi:
fix: Fix universal checkpoint for ZeRO Stage 3 with multiple subgroups

Fix universal checkpoint conversion and loading failures when using ZeRO Stage 3 with multiple parameter subgroups (e.g., large models or low sub_group_size settings).

- Updated extract_zero_shards_stage3 to iterate over all subgroups instead of assuming a single group at index 0, preventing data loss and dimension errors
- Modified _merge_zero3_slice_files to accept param_keys instead of flattened param_shapes for correct parallel processing
- Fixed checkpoint loading to properly reconstruct optimizer state from multiple subgroups using param_names mapping
- Resolved file corruption issue when load_universal_checkpoint is True by ensuring only rank 0 writes the universal checkpoint file
- Added comprehensive tests for multi-subgroup scenarios with varying sub_group_size values

This addresses the RuntimeError where start + length exceeds dimension size due to incorrect offset calculations when multiple subgroups exist, and prevents checkpoint file corruption from concurrent writes.
messages.claude:
fix: support multiple sub-groups in ZeRO-3 universal checkpoint

The previous universal checkpoint implementation for ZeRO-3 assumed a
single parameter sub-group, which caused failures (and silent data loss)
when models were large enough to be partitioned into multiple sub-groups.

What:
- ds_to_universal.py: iterate over each sub-group when extracting and
  merging zero shards instead of only indexing state[0] /
  fp32_flat_groups[0]; collect param keys across all sub-groups for
  merging.
- stage3.py: load universal checkpoint per sub-group by walking
  fp16_groups / fp32_partitioned_groups_flat and rehydrating optimizer
  state per sub-group (step, exp_avg, exp_avg_sq, param_groups) rather
  than concatenating all layers into a single tensor; drop the
  param_shapes argument since param_names is now used to locate each
  parameter's shard.
- engine.py / mics.py: thread param_names through Stage3ZeroOptimizer
  and MiCS_Optimizer so the loader can map params to names; universal
  checkpoints now load the single shared "zero_pp_rank_0" file via
  _get_all_ckpt_names instead of per-rank files, avoiding concurrent
  writes corrupting the file when load_checkpoint is true.

Why:
Issue #7584 reported that ds_to_universal.py crashed with
`RuntimeError: start (0) + length (...) exceeds dimension size (...)`
when multiple sub-groups were present, because the extractor assumed a
single flat group and walked past the end of the tensor. Beyond the
crash, the loader also silently dropped optimizer state for any
sub-group beyond the first, and per-rank checkpoint files could be
corrupted by concurrent writes during universal checkpoint saving.
Handling sub-groups end to end (extraction, merge, and load) and
consolidating on a single shared file fixes both the data-loss and
file-corruption issues.

Tests: extended test_universal_checkpoint.py with a sub_group_size
parametrization and a 2-layer SimpleModel plus update_gathered_stage3_optimizer to verify multi-sub-group round-trips across
dp world-size changes.
messages.minimax:
fix: handle multiple sub-groups in ZeRO-3 universal checkpoint

The previous ZeRO-3 universal checkpoint implementation did not properly handle multiple sub-groups (when sub_group_size is configured), causing data loss. Additionally, all ranks would write to the same checkpoint file when load_universal_checkpoint was enabled, leading to file corruption.

- Fixed extract_zero_shards_stage3 to iterate over each sub-group's parameter shapes and state instead of assuming a single flat state dict at index [0]
- Fixed _merge_zero3_slice_files to work with per-subgroup parameter keys instead of flattened keys
- Fixed _get_ckpt_name to use distinct filenames per rank instead of the same "zero_pp_rank_0" for universal checkpoints
- Fixed _get_all_ckpt_names to return only the first checkpoint file when loading universal checkpoint, preventing duplicate loading
- Fixed load_hp_checkpoint_state_from_checkpoint_dir_stage3 to correctly map parameters by name across sub-groups instead of concatenating all parameters at index [0]
- Added param_names propagation through Stage3ZeroOptimizer and MiCS_Optimizer to enable named parameter lookup during checkpoint loading
- Added sub_group_size test parameter and update_gathered_stage3_optimizer helper to properly verify multi-subgroup optimizer state reorganization
```

fix: Remove redundant dtype parameter from report_ipg_memory_usage calls

The report_ipg_memory_usage function signature only accepts two parameters
(message and numel), but the code was incorrectly passing a third dtype
parameter. This caused a key error crash when using ZeRO 2 with bfloat16
parameters and sequence parallelism. Remove the extra dtype argument to
match the function's expected signature and prevent the crash.

Fixes #7607
messages.claude:
fix: remove param.dtype argument from report_ipg_memory_usage calls in ZeRO stage 1/2

Fixes #7607

When training with ZeRO 2, bfloat16 parameters, sequence parallelism, and
no torch autocast, a KeyError crash occurs inside
report_ipg_memory_usage. The root cause is that report_ipg_memory_usage
was being invoked with param.dtype as an extra positional argument, which
is not a valid parameter for that method and produced a key error when
resolving the bucket dtype under these configurations.

The two call sites in reduce_independent_p_g_buckets_and_remove_grads are
updated to drop the trailing param.dtype argument so the call matches the
method signature and the bucket lookup succeeds regardless of parameter
dtype, restoring training stability for the affected configurations.
messages.minimax:
Fix key error in report_ipg_memory_usage with bfloat16 params

When using ZeRO 2 with bfloat16 parameters and sequence parallelism
(without torch autocast), report_ipg_memory_usage crashes with a key
error. The dtype argument is not required for memory reporting, so
remove it to fix the crash.

Fixes #7607

[aten] 8 bytes aligned vector loads for bf16 and fp16 dtypes in torch.cat (#150233)

Enable aligned vector loading for 2 bytes datatypes in torch.cat. Specifically:
1. reduce the vector length to 8 bytes for 2-byte types (fp16, bf16 etc)
2. enable through a conditional template

The reason why 8-byte vector loading was chosen for fp16 and bf16:
16-byte load results in heavier register overheads (i.e. 4 register per load for fp32 -> 8 register per load for fp16). Therefore, to employ the benefits of vectorized loading, we reduced ALIGNED_VEC_LOAD_BYTES to 8 for fp16 and bf16

### Perf testing code:

```
# pyre-strict
from typing import List, Optional, Tuple

import click
import pandas as pd

import torch

# @manual=//triton:triton
import triton

# CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICEs=7 buck2 run @mode/opt //scripts/zhaozhu:cat_bench

@click.command()
@click.option("--data-type", type=str, default="bf16")
@click.option("--return-result", type=bool, default=False)
def main(
    data_type: str,
    return_result: bool,
) -> Optional[Tuple[List[triton.testing.Benchmark], List[pd.DataFrame]]]:
    torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32 = True
    torch.backends.cuda.matmul.allow_tf32 = True
    if data_type == "fp32":
        dtype = torch.float32
    elif data_type == "fp16":
        dtype = torch.float16
    elif data_type == "bf16":
        dtype = torch.bfloat16
    else:
        raise ValueError(f"Unsupported data type: {data_type}.")

    D1 = int(torch.randint(low=10000, high=50000, size=(1,)).item())
    D2 = int(torch.randint(low=100, high=1000, size=(1,)).item())
    D3 = int(torch.randint(low=500, high=1000, size=(1,)).item())

    configs: List[triton.testing.Benchmark] = [
        triton.testing.Benchmark(
            x_names=["B"],
            x_vals=[100, 1000, 10000, 20000],
            line_arg="provider",
            line_vals=["pt_eager", "copy"],
            line_names=["pt_eager", "copy"],
            styles=[("blue", "-"), ("green", "-"), ("red", "-")],
            ylabel="ms",
            plot_name=f"torch-cat-D1-{D1}-D2-{D2}-D3-{D3}-dtype-{dtype}",
            args={
                "D1": D1,
                "D2": D2,
                "D3": D3,
                "dtype": dtype,
            },
        )
    ]

    @triton.testing.perf_report(configs)
    def bench_cat(
        B: int,
        D1: int,
        D2: int,
        D3: int,
        dtype: torch.dtype,
        provider: str,
    ) -> float:
        warmup = 10
        rep = 3

        tensors = []

        a = torch.empty(
            # (B, 30108),
            (B, D1),
            dtype=dtype,
            device=torch.device("cuda"),
        ).uniform_(-1.0, 1.0)
        b = torch.empty(
            # (B, 624),
            (B, D2),
            dtype=dtype,
            device=torch.device("cuda"),
        ).uniform_(-1.0, 1.0)
        c = torch.empty(
            # (B, 772),
            (B, D3),
            dtype=dtype,
            device=torch.device("cuda"),
        ).uniform_(-1.0, 1.0)

        tensors = [a, b, c]

        total_cols: int = int(a.shape[1] + b.shape[1] + c.shape[1])

        def torch_copy(
            tensors: List[torch.Tensor], is_inplace: bool = True
        ) -> torch.Tensor:
            f = torch.zeros([B, total_cols], dtype=dtype, device=torch.device("cuda"))
            col_idx = 0
            for t in tensors:
                temp = f[:, col_idx : col_idx + t.shape[1]]
                if is_inplace:
                    temp.copy_(t)
                else:
                    f[:, col_idx : col_idx + t.shape[1]] = t
                col_idx += t.shape[1]
            return f

        def torch_cat(tensors: List[torch.Tensor]) -> torch.Tensor:
            return torch.cat(tensors, dim=1)

        ref = torch_cat(tensors)
        real = torch_copy(tensors, is_inplace=False)

        torch.testing.assert_allclose(ref, real)

        if provider == "pt_eager":
            fn = lambda: torch_cat(tensors)  # noqa E731
            ms = triton.testing.do_bench(fn, warmup=warmup, rep=rep)
            return ms
        elif provider == "stack":

            def torch_stack(tensors: List[torch.Tensor]) -> torch.Tensor:
                return torch.stack(tensors, dim=1).view(-1, total_cols)

            fn = lambda: torch_stack(tensors)
            ms = triton.testing.do_bench(fn, warmup=warmup, rep=rep)
            return ms
        elif provider == "copy":
            fn = lambda: torch_copy(tensors)
            ms = triton.testing.do_bench(fn, warmup=warmup, rep=rep)
            return ms
        else:
            raise ValueError(f"unsupported provider: {provider}")

    df = bench_cat.run(print_data=True, return_df=return_result)

    if return_result:
        return configs, df

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

### Problem
Running `nvshmem_all_to_all_vdev` on 4 x H100s (fully connected with NVSwitch).

Issue #7640: [BUG] Integer overflow in FusedAdam silently prevents weight updates for large tensors (>= 2^31 elements)
## Describe the bug
DeepSpeed's `FusedAdam` optimizer silently fails to update model parameters if a single optimizer param group contains a tensor with size > 2^31 - 1 (or `INT_MAX`).

### Symptoms

This issue was discovered while training a ~2.4B model on a single GPU using ZeRO stage 2 (the ZeRO here is not necessary and only for testing before launching multi-node training). The training steps appeared normal at first glance, but I later found that the model weights and Adam params were never updated. The same training configuration works correctly with 2 or more GPUs.

### Root Cause Analysis

The issue likely stems from an integer overflow in `csrc/adam/multi_tensor_apply.cuh`, which ultimately causes the `FusedAdam` operator to malfunction.

1.  The `TensorListMetadata` struct defines an array `int sizes[...]` to store the number of elements for each tensor, which uses **32-bit signed integers**.
2.  In the `multi_tensor_apply` function, the tensor size (`tensor_lists[0][t].numel()`, which is of type `int64_t`) is assigned to this `int` array. When `numel` is `2^31` or greater, this assignment overflows, and the stored value becomes negative.
3.  The wrapper `multi_tensor_adam_cuda` correctly detects that the tensor size requires 64-bit indexing and instantiates the `AdamFunctor` kernel with `index_t = int64_t`.
4.  However, inside the kernel, when the corrupted negative size is read from `tl.sizes` into the 64-bit variable `index_t n`, the main processing loop `for (index_t i_start = 0; i_start < n; ...)` immediately terminates because `n` is negative, so the condition `i_start < n` is false from the start.

This causes the kernel to perform **_no operations_**, incorrectly leaving the parameters and optimizer states unchanged.

The bug can be reproduced with the following minimal script, which directly invokes the `FusedAdam` CUDA operator.

    ```python
    # N_PARAMS = 2147483647 # This works correctly

    N_FRONT = min(N_PARAMS, 8)


    if __name__ == "__main__":
        torch.manual_seed(42)

        fused_adam_cuda = FusedAdamBuilder().load()

fix(adam): use int64_t for tensor sizes in multi_tensor_apply to prevent overflow for large tensors

The `sizes` array in `TensorListMetadata` was declared as `int` (32-bit),
which silently overflowed when a tensor contained >= 2^31 elements. The
overflowed (negative) value was then read into the 64-bit loop bound
`index_t n`, causing the `for (index_t i_start = 0; i_start < n; ...)`
loop to terminate immediately and skip all weight updates.

Promoting `sizes` to `int64_t` preserves the full numel value so the
AdamFunctor kernel iterates over the complete tensor as intended.

Fixes #7640

Change the `sizes` array type from `int` to `int64_t` in `TensorListMetadata` struct to fix integer overflow when processing tensors with >= 2^31 elements.

The bug caused FusedAdam to silently skip weight updates for large tensors because:
1. `int sizes[]` overflowed when storing tensor element counts >= 2^31
2. The corrupted negative value caused the kernel loop to immediately terminate
3. Parameters and optimizer states remained unchanged without any error

This fix ensures proper 64-bit indexing support throughout the multi-tensor apply pipeline.

fix: change sizes array from int to int64_t to prevent overflow for large tensors

The `TensorListMetadata::sizes` array was declared as `int` (32-bit), but tensor sizes can exceed `INT_MAX` (2^31 - 1). Changing `sizes` to `int64_t` allows the array to correctly store tensor sizes for tensors with up to 2^63 - 1 elements.
```

model dtypes on ROCm, since bf16 was not being relaxed despite the same

expands coverage so the test suite reliably validates the bf16 path
referenced in the issue.

the Ulysses-Offload blog entry.

messages.kimi:
What (Summary):
The changes fix a bug in ZeRO++ (zero_hpz_partition_size) where:
1. `has_been_updated` flag wasn't being passed to `_partition_param_sec()` in `partition_parameters.py`
2. `ds_secondary_tensor` wasn't properly handling gradients during copy operations
3. Secondary tensors weren't being invalidated during checkpoint epilogue

Why (Rationale):
Issue #7606 reports that when using ZeRO++ with `zero_hpz_partition_size` set, the loss of the first step (or first step after loading checkpoint) is abnormally high. This happens because:
- The secondary tensor partitioning wasn't respecting the `has_been_updated` flag, causing stale data issues
- Gradient tracking on secondary tensors during copy operations could cause incorrect gradient accumulation
- Missing invalidation of secondary tensors during checkpoint events led to inconsistent state

Type: fix

fix: Fix ZeRO++ high loss issue on first step after checkpoint load

Fix incorrect parameter partitioning and secondary tensor handling in ZeRO++ when zero_hpz_partition_size is set.

- Pass has_been_updated flag to _partition_param_sec() to ensure consistent partitioning behavior between primary and secondary tensors
- Wrap secondary tensor copy operation in torch.no_grad() context to prevent unintended gradient tracking on ds_secondary_tensor
- Add invalidate_secondary_tensor() call in checkpoint_event_epilogue() to ensure secondary tensors are properly reset after checkpoint operations

These changes fix the bug where the first training step after loading a checkpoint would produce abnormally high loss values when using ZeRO++ with hierarchical partitioning (zero_hpz_partition_size). The issue was caused by stale secondary tensor data and incorrect gradient state being carried over from checkpoint loading.
messages.claude:
fix: prevent stale secondary tensor from corrupting first-step loss with zero_hpz_partition_size

When zero_hpz_partition_size is set (ZeRO++), the first training step after a
checkpoint load produced an abnormally high loss. The root cause is that the
secondary tensor retained stale/incorrect data across the checkpoint event:
the secondary partition was copied without an explicit no_grad context, which
could let ds_secondary_tensor pick up gradients/autograd state and leave it in
an inconsistent state, and the secondary tensor was never invalidated during
checkpoint epilogue, so a load reused stale values.

- Wrap the secondary tensor copy in _partition_param_sec under torch.no_grad()
  to guarantee ds_secondary_tensor.requires_grad stays False and the copy does
  not thread through autograd.
- Plumb has_been_updated into the _partition_param_sec call in _partition so
  the partition path honors the caller's update intent.
- Call invalidate_secondary_tensor() in checkpoint_event_epilogue so loaded
  checkpoints do not reuse stale secondary partitions.
- Add ws4_model_checkpoint_zeropp fixture and TestZeROPPLoadCheckpoint cases
  (test_load_zeropp_model, test_load_zeropp_checkpoint) covering model-only and
  full checkpoint load with zero_hpz_partition_size=2 to guard against
  regression of issue #7606.
messages.minimax:
fix: ensure requires_grad stays false on secondary tensors in ZeRO++

When `zero_hpz_partition_size` is set, the secondary tensor copy operation was allowing gradient tracking to leak through, causing the first training step or first step after checkpoint load to produce abnormally high loss.

- Wrap secondary tensor copy in `torch.no_grad()` to guarantee `ds_secondary_tensor.requires_grad` remains false
- Pass `has_been_updated` flag to `_partition_param_sec` so partition logic has correct state
- Call `invalidate_secondary_tensor()` in `checkpoint_event_epilogue` to clear stale state on checkpoint load
- Add tests for ZeRO++ checkpoint save/load with `zero_hpz_partition_size=2`

Fixes #7606.

fix: Fix assertion failure in ZeRO-3 swap when no tensors need swapping

The assertion `len(swap_tensors) == aio_handle.wait()` fails when `swap_tensors` is empty because `aio_handle.wait()` internally asserts `_num_pending_ops > 0`. This occurs in ZeRO-3 training with libaio-dev installed when no parameters need to be swapped in during optimizer state management.

Add a guard to only call `aio_handle.wait()` when there are actually pending swap operations, preventing the assertion failure during LLM training with ZeRO-3 offload.

Fixes #7703
messages.minimax:
fix: avoid assertion failure when no swap tensors are pending in ZeRO-3

When using ZeRO-3 with libaio-dev, _swap_in_fp16_params could hit assertion `_num_pending_ops > 0` in aio_handle.wait() if swap_tensors was empty, causing training to fail. The assertion is now only evaluated when len(swap_tensors) > 0.

Fixes #7703
messages.claude:
fix: avoid aio_handle.wait() assertion when no swap tensors are pending

Guard the assertion `len(swap_tensors) == aio_handle.wait()` so it only
runs when `swap_tensors` is non-empty. Previously the assertion executed
unconditionally, including on paths where no async swap operations had
been submitted. This triggered
`int deepspeed_io_handle_t::wait(): Assertion '_num_pending_ops > 0'`
inside libaio whenever `wait()` was called with zero pending ops, which
in practice happened during ZeRO-3 training with libaio-dev installed
(see issue #7703): the swap-in path for fp16 params could reach this
point with an empty `swap_tensors` list, causing the C++ assertion to
abort the process and preventing training from even starting.

By skipping both the assertion and the underlying `wait()` call when
there are no tensors to wait on, we match the actual semantics of the
async I/O handle and let ZeRO-3 + libaio configurations proceed.

messages.claude:
fix: guard against None grad in backward prologue hook

When DeepCompile is enabled (e.g. training Llama2), the backward engine
passes multiple losses to the backward graph, one of which is None and
not actually consumed by the graph. PR #7665 registered a per-tensor
backward hook that scales the grad by gradient_accumulation_steps, but
that hook assumed the incoming grad was always a valid tensor. With
DeepCompile breaking that assumption, the division
`grad / self.gradient_accumulation_steps()` raised
`TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for /: 'NoneType' and 'int'`
and aborted training.

Return the None grad early so unused grads flow through the hook
untouched, restoring compatibility with DeepCompile's multi-loss
backward graph.

Fixes #7708
messages.minimax:
fix: handle None grad in _backward_prologue_per_tensor

When DeepCompile is enabled, the backward engine may pass a None grad to the backward hook. This None value then reaches _backward_prologue_per_tensor which attempts to divide it by gradient_accumulation_steps(), causing a TypeError.

This fix adds a guard to return early when grad is None, preventing the exception and allowing training to complete normally.

Fixes #7708
messages.kimi:
fix: Handle None gradients in _backward_prologue_per_tensor hook

Fixes #7708

The backward hook added in #7665 to scale gradients by accumulation steps assumes the gradient is always a valid tensor. However, when using DeepCompile, the backward engine may pass None gradients for losses not used by the graph, causing a TypeError when attempting to divide None by an integer.

Add a None check at the beginning of _backward_prologue_per_tensor to return early when the gradient is None, preventing the division operation from failing.
